title: The Great Synagogue and Będzin’s Houses of Prayer
summary: Synagogues and prayer houses were central to religious and communal life, and the book records both their artistic richness and their destruction.
editorialContent:
![The Great Synagogue in Będzin before its destruction](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/11/B%C4%99dzin_-_Zamek_obronny_z_XIVw..jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)
## A synagogue at the heart of communal life

In Będzin, the Great Synagogue was more than a building for worship. It was a landmark of Jewish communal life: a place for prayer and ceremony, but also a space where religious tradition met public affairs. The memorial book, *Pinkas Bendin*, remembers it as the “great synagogue” and includes a caption identifying it in 1910. The caption preserves the community’s image of the building, though it does not by itself prove which surviving photograph shows it. ([Great Synagogue](\/communities\/bedzin\/records\/mention_582ad9f8e21d85bb1d340fda))

The book places the synagogue within a wider network of houses of prayer and study. Its account recalls an earlier Będzin synagogue where, in 1591, court proceedings took place and rules were posted. It also says the wooden synagogue was dismantled in 1881 and a new building erected on the same site. The Great Synagogue thus represented not the whole of religious life, but one prominent institution within a community whose worship and learning were spread among several venues. ([Będzin synagogue](\/communities\/bedzin\/records\/mention_77b0376e0cfb52767f99ab28))

The memorial book’s portrait of daily religious life makes that distinction vivid. The Great Synagogue was especially associated with communal occasions and public ceremonies; nearby, the Large Bet Midrash offered a more everyday setting for prayer and study. Its account describes worshippers arriving and leaving through the day, some hurrying back to work, while others studied Talmud or Mishnah. The contrast is not between religious and secular life, but between different spaces serving different rhythms of the same community. ([Synagogue](\/communities\/bedzin\/records\/mention_e17b35e7db52494712609645))

The wider historical record adds scale to this local memory. Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos notes that Jews made up about 45 percent of Będzin’s population in 1931, and describes the community’s charitable institutions, political movements and youth organisations. In such a large and active Jewish population, a central synagogue could serve as a conspicuous public symbol, while smaller prayer houses and study halls sustained more intimate, routine forms of religious life. ([Yad Vashem’s Będzin entry](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=150))

## Painted walls, local artists

The synagogue’s interior decoration connected religious space to artistic life. *Pinkas Bendin* dates the major painting and decorative work to 1925–26, naming Mosze Apelboim, Shmuel Cygler and Chaim Hanft. The book describes Apelboim’s work on the eastern wall and Cygler’s on the western wall, and recalls Hanft’s metalwork. It also notes that reproductions of the synagogue’s art were held in Jerusalem, at the Tel Aviv Museum, and at YIVO. These details make the decoration more than ornament in retrospect: it was a locally remembered artistic achievement, created by Jewish artists and craftsmen for a communal institution. ([Będzin synagogue](\/communities\/bedzin\/records\/mention_38b79c7b54079aea73188220); [Moshe Opelboim](\/communities\/bedzin\/records\/mention_7e61a6e1cfe74da211ceb11f); [Samuel Zigler](\/communities\/bedzin\/records\/mention_d806cc72150f303bcc19447); [Chaim Hanft](\/communities\/bedzin\/records\/mention_bf51a496a0e3c51484ae41cb))

The names and spellings vary across the records: Apelboim also appears as Apelbaum, and Cygler as Zigler or Cygler in different accounts and captions. The memorial book’s artist biography says Apelboim came to Będzin in 1925 and worked there with Cygler and Hanft. It also remembers Apelboim as a painter who had studied in London and worked in Warsaw. The book’s account identifies him as born in Amshinov (Mszczonów); the supplied records also associate him with Warsaw and the Royal Academy of Arts in London. These biographical details belong to the book’s account, not independent confirmation of every stage of his career. ([Będzin Writers and Artists](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/bedzin/bed098.html))

For the community that commissioned and used it, the decoration made the Great Synagogue a distinctly Będzin achievement. The book’s language of pride is plain: it recalls the building’s spacious interior, its substantial benches, its cantor and choir, and its painted walls. A photograph captioned as the Great Synagogue in 1936 and images identified as sections of its murals help anchor that remembrance in visual evidence. Yet the pictures and the later descriptions do not restore the whole building; they preserve fragments of an interior whose significance came from its use as well as its appearance. ([The Great Synagogue and the Large Bet Midrash](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/bedzin/bed136.html); [photograph of a synagogue wall painting](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/Bedzin/BedPh041.html))

## A public place, not only a prayer hall

The memorial book remembers the Great Synagogue as a place where the community gathered for special occasions. It names sermons connected with the Polish national holiday of 11 November, as well as observances such as the 20th of Tammuz. The synagogue’s public role did not erase religious divisions or the many smaller institutions of Będzin. Rather, it offered a shared setting for occasions on which communal life became visible beyond the daily routines of individual prayer houses.

Other records point to the breadth of that religious landscape. The memorial book mentions a Large Bet Midrash beside the Great Synagogue, and recalls a broader network of synagogues and prayer rooms. Among the individuals connected with this world are Rabbi Grossman, Fiowel Rapaport and Rabbi Israel the Cantor; the book’s recollections also mention Moses Opelboim, Samuel Zigler and Maled Applebaum in connection with the synagogue. The evidence supplied here does not establish a complete map of Będzin’s houses of prayer or resolve every person’s precise role. It does show why “the synagogue” should not be mistaken for the entirety of religious life in town.

## Fire and rupture

The memorial book’s accounts place the synagogue’s destruction in the first days of German occupation. Some passages describe the fire during the Nazi invasion; another remembers the synagogue going up in flames. Those recollections establish the event’s place in community memory, but they do not all give an exact date or identical account of what happened around the building. ([Nazi invasion of Będzin](\/communities\/bedzin\/records\/mention_91c152d186b1459ef5f7a6d0); [Synagogue fire](\/communities\/bedzin\/records\/mention_77bfa222006365b90e781973))

Independent sources narrow the chronology. Yad Vashem dates the German occupation of Będzin to 5 September 1939 and says the Germans set fire to the central synagogue a few days later. It reports that the fire spread to nearby houses and that about 60 Jews died when they were prevented from escaping. A separate Yad Vashem entry gives 4 September as the date of occupation and 9 September for the synagogue fire; these records differ on the occupation date, while agreeing that the synagogue was burned in the first days of occupation. The difference should remain visible rather than being smoothed into false precision. ([Yad Vashem’s Będzin entry](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=150); [Yad Vashem’s town entry](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/odot_pdf/Microsoft%20Word%20-%20836.pdf))

The memorial book describes the aftermath in the language of loss: the paintings were destroyed, and the great building became a heap of stones. It also remembers survivors taking bricks from the ruins to light Sabbath candles. That act, as the book tells it, joined the remains of a public institution to the most intimate practice of home observance. It is a remembered image, not a substitute for the historical account of the fire and the people killed.

The burning was therefore both physical destruction and a rupture in the familiar geography of Jewish Będzin. The Great Synagogue had gathered worshippers and marked public occasions; its neighboring houses of prayer and study sustained daily religious life. Occupation brought violence to those spaces and to the people who depended on them. The community’s memory preserves the artists’ names, the walls they decorated, and the prayers once heard there. The independent record confirms the fire’s place in the occupation’s opening days, while *Pinkas Bendin* tells us what the destroyed synagogue meant to those who remembered it.
